query: Earlier refractory high-entropy alloys illustrate persistent trade-offs: MoNbTaW and MoNbTaVW retained good yield strength from 600 to 1600 °C, with MoNbTaVW reaching 842 MPa at 1000 °C, but both had poor room-temperature fracture toughness and high density; HfNbTaTiZr showed room-temperature ductility above 50% and a yield strength of 929 MPa but only 295 MPa at 1000 °C; and as-cast HfMoTaTiZr achieved about 1600 MPa at room temperature and 855 MPa at elevated temperature but retained a density of 10.21 g cm−3. Given the constraint that density must be reduced without sacrificing the strong room- and high-temperature mechanical performance of as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, what single intervention should be tested? Provide a mechanistic hypothesis, predicted outcomes relative to the as-cast baseline, explicit temperature and loading boundary conditions, supporting evidence from the preceding RHEA results, and a controlled experiment with quantitative rejection criteria that could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Partial substitution of a fraction of the heavy Hf atoms in as‐cast HfMoTaTiZr with a low‐density element such as Al will reduce the alloy’s overall density while preserving its high yield strength at both room and elevated temperatures.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr with a density of 10.21 g/cm³, ~1600 MPa yield strength at room temperature, and ~855 MPa yield strength at elevated temperatures (~1000 °C)
generation.intervention: Replace approximately 10–20 atomic percent of Hf with Al (i.e. a partial Hf→Al substitution) in the alloy composition to form a modified alloy (e.g., Hf1-xAlxMoTaTiZr with x ≈ 0.1–0.2).
generation.conditions: Mechanical testing under uniaxial tensile loading at room temperature and at 1000 °C; microstructural evaluations post-casting to verify phase stability and homogeneity.
generation.structural_mediator: The alloy’s single-phase body-centered cubic (BCC) solid-solution structure, maintained by high-entropy stabilization, is expected to be modified by the Al addition without leading to deleterious intermetallic precipitates.
generation.mechanism: The low atomic mass and relatively small atomic radius of Al compared to Hf will lower the overall density. Simultaneously, because Al can be incorporated as a solid-solution element, it is anticipated to contribute to solid-solution strengthening without severe compromises to ductility or high-temperature strength. The maintained BCC phase should continue to facilitate the robust dislocation mechanisms that underpin both room-temperature toughness and high-temperature yield strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy should exhibit a notable reduction in overall density (targeting a decrease from ~10.21 g/cm³ to a lower value) while retaining room-temperature and ~1000 °C yield strengths within approximately 10% of the baseline (i.e. ~1400–1600 MPa at room temperature and ~800–855 MPa at 1000 °C).
generation.baseline: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr with an approximate density of 10.21 g/cm³, 1600 MPa room-temperature yield strength, and 855 MPa yield strength at elevated temperatures.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is tested under tensile loading at room temperature and at an elevated temperature of approximately 1000 °C. The density reduction target and retention of yield strength (within ~10% variation) serve as the performance boundaries.
generation.uncertainty: It is uncertain how the Al substitution might affect phase stability and the fine balance of solid-solution strengthening at very high temperatures; minor reductions in yield strength could occur if the substitution alters dislocation behavior or local bonding significantly.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate a series of alloys with the composition Hf1-xAlxMoTaTiZr with x = 0 (control), 0.1, and 0.2. Process them under identical as-cast conditions. Characterize the microstructure via XRD and SEM to ensure phase homogeneity. Conduct uniaxial tensile tests at room temperature and at 1000 °C to measure yield strengths. Determine the density of each alloy using Archimedes’ method.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-substituted alloys do not exhibit a significant reduction in density relative to the control (i.e., less than an approximate 5–10% decrease) or if either the room-temperature or elevated-temperature yield strengths drop by more than ~10% relative to the as-cast HfMoTaTiZr baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Effects of Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr on Mechanical Properties of Equiatomic Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr Alloys

Abstract: AbstractNowadays refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are regarded as great candidates for the replacement of superalloys at high temperature. To design a RHEA, one must understand the pros and cons of every refractory element. However, the elemental effect on mechanical properties remains unclear. In this study, the subtraction method was applied on equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys to discover the role of each element, and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were fabricated and analyzed. The microstructure and mechanical properties of each alloy at the as-cast state were examined. The solid solution phase formation rule and the solution strengthening effect are also discussed. Finally, the mechanism of how Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr affect the HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys was established after comparing the properties of these alloys.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, refractory high-entropy alloys, alloys design, elevated-temperature yield strength, solid solution strengthening effect

Conclusions: The equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy was chosen

Microstructure and Mechanical Properties of TaNbVTiAlx Refractory High-Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractA series of TaNbVTiAlx (x = 0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8, and 1.0) refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) with high specific strength and reasonable plasticity were prepared using powder metallurgy (P/M) technology. This paper studied their microstructure and compression properties. The results show that all the TaNbVTiAlx RHEAs exhibited a single BCC solid solution microstructure with no elemental segregation. The P/M TaNbVTiAlx RHEAs showed excellent room-temperature specific strength (207.11 MPa*cm3/g) and high-temperature specific strength (88.37 MPa*cm3/g at 900 °C and 16.03 MPa*cm3/g at 1200 °C), with reasonable plasticity, suggesting that these RHEAs have potential to be applied at temperatures >1200 °C. The reasons for the excellent mechanical properties of P/M TaNbVTiAl0.2 RHEA were the uniform microstructure and solid solution strengthening effect.Keywords: high-entropy alloy, refractory alloy, powder metallurgy, specific strength, ductile
